desc: MITRE is the priority institution of this domain and, on the board's premise, the structural heart of the concealment architecture. It was incorporated as a nonprofit on 21 July 1958, spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory's Division 6 to carry the systems engineering of the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment continental air defence system - Robert Everett and 485 other Lincoln Laboratory staff walked across at founding. It was created by the Air Force, explicitly on the RAND model, to be a permanent nonprofit answerable to a military customer rather than to a university. It now operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for the Department of Defense under the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and IRS with VA, SSA and Commerce as co-sponsors; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS S&T, created 5 March 2009; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence for NIST, created 19 September 2014. NSEC alone was funded at roughly 1.43 billion dollars in FY2024. MITRE also administers JASON, the government's most sensitive standing scientific advisory panel. Its revenue passed 2.37 billion dollars in 2023. The reason MITRE, and not Lockheed or Northrop, is the load-bearing node is the combination in one organisation of: sponsorship by both the defence and intelligence establishment and the civil aviation regulator that owns the radar picture of American airspace; FAR-granted access to both government compartmented data and prime contractor proprietary data; contractor records status that puts its files outside FOIA; a governing board repeatedly chaired or vice-chaired by former Principal Deputy Directors of National Intelligence; and a chief executive imported directly from Battelle. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison sent MITRE a 10-page legislative production request demanding an accounting of UAP records, anomalous aerospace or undersea events, recovered materials and technologies of unknown origin, legacy crash-retrieval or reverse-engineering programmes, Special and Controlled Access Programs, sensor data, materials analysis and classification guides, reaching back to 1930. MITRE's response was that it was reviewing its archives and that 'if any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work' - which restates the exact problem: an FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor, not to Congress.

claims.text: Federal Acquisition Regulation 35.017(a)(2) states that an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.'

MITRE operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center (DoD), the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development (FAA), the Center for Enterprise Modernization (Treasury/IRS, co-sponsored by VA, SSA and Commerce), the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute (DHS), the Health FFRDC (HHS), and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC (NIST).

The DHS-MITRE sponsoring agreement for HS SEDI obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data ... including that which is not normally available to non-government organizations' (Section 5(h)).

Under Section 6(b)(9) of the same agreement, the DHS Executive Agent 'Reviews and approves the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications' - meaning the sponsoring agency, not MITRE, controls whether MITRE's work product can be released.

Section 5(j)(iv) of the same agreement requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) secrecy terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2)' - the clause that preserves the right to make disclosures to Congress essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.

Section 9(g)(2) of the same agreement states that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law' - a protection extended to MITRE's own personnel but expressly withheld from its subcontractors and consultants.

Section 5(a) of the same agreement states that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects and shall strictly comply with the provisions of the National Industrial Security Program ... as set forth in DOD Directive 5220.22-M as amended.'

On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison transmitted a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE president Mark Peters and general counsel Christopher Land, setting the relevant search period as 'January 1, 1930, to the present.'

The Burlison interrogatories demand that MITRE identify all Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, Managed-Need-To-Know codewords and DOE SIGMA categories it participated in or supported in connection with UAP-related records, and state for each 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify any nondisclosure agreement, indoctrination record or sponsor communication 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress, Inspectors General, AARO, NARA, federal law enforcement, or appropriate cleared oversight officials.'

The Burlison interrogatories ask MITRE to identify 'any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems, Bigelow Aerospace or its successors/affiliates.'

Burlison's accompanying statement of 26 May 2026 says FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records - especially records Congress has directed to be identified, preserved, reviewed, and transferred for public release.'

MITRE's public response, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets'; a member of Burlison's staff told the same outlet that the letter was informed by 'advice from many whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations, and those working at FFRDCs.'

MITRE's certification of search methodology, records-location index, preservation hold and production of unclassified responsive records - all demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks from 22 May 2026 - have not been placed on the public record.

dossier.denialPosture: MITRE has not denied holding UAP-related records. Its only public statement on the Burlison inquiry, given through a spokesperson to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was that it was reviewing its archives and that 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' No certification, denial of possession, or records-location index has been made public.
dossier.narrative:
MITRE occupies a category that exists nowhere else in the federal enterprise. It manufactures nothing, competes for nothing, and sells nothing. It exists to hold institutional memory and technical judgement on behalf of government sponsors, and the Federal Acquisition Regulation builds that role out of a single privilege: an FFRDC 'has access, beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship, to Government and supplier data, including sensitive and proprietary data, and to employees and installations equipment and real property.' That sentence, FAR 35.017(a)(2), is the load-bearing beam of this dossier. Everything a prime contractor knows about its own black programmes, and everything the government knows about the prime, can lawfully sit inside the FFRDC that sits between them.

MITRE currently operates six FFRDCs: the National Security Engineering Center for DoD; the Center for Advanced Aviation System Development for the FAA; the Center for Enterprise Modernization for Treasury and the IRS, co-sponsored by Veterans Affairs, the Social Security Administration and Commerce; the Homeland Security Systems Engineering and Development Institute for DHS; the Health FFRDC for HHS; and the National Cybersecurity FFRDC for NIST. Its own fact sheet notes there are only forty-two FFRDCs in total and that operating six of them is 'a high honor.' The relevant point for this board is not prestige but coverage: one nonprofit sits inside the defence establishment, the intelligence-adjacent national security enterprise, and the civil aviation regulator that owns the primary radar picture of American airspace.

The governing document that shows how this works in practice is the FY2009 sponsoring agreement between DHS and MITRE for HS SEDI, signed by MITRE's president and by the Acting Under Secretary for Science and Technology on 13 March 2009. It is worth reading as a specification for exactly the kind of custody problem this board is mapping. Section 3 states that SEDI's work 'will often require privileged access to information, including sensitive Government information and industry proprietary data not normally available to non-Government organizations.' Section 5(h) obliges the sponsors to 'provide access to classified and sensitive data, facilities, plans and related information, including proprietary data.' Section 6(c)(9) records the routine practice: 'Ordinarily, sponsors release classified, privileged, no-contractor, and other sensitive material directly to SEDI.' Section 5(a) states plainly that 'The SEDI will work on many classified and highly sensitive projects.'

Then the agreement closes the loop on disclosure. Section 6(b)(9) gives the DHS Executive Agent authority to review and approve 'the classification, publication, and distribution of SEDI publications.' Section 9(g) defines 'Privileged Information' so broadly that it captures every deliverable, note, lab record, test result and analysis MITRE produces for the sponsor, and forbids disclosure except as required by law or 'as expressly authorized in writing by the DHS Executive Agent.' Section 9(g)(2) then carves back the whistleblower statutes, stating that 'Signing this Agreement does not bar disclosures to Congress or to an authorized official of an executive agency or the Department of Justice that are essential to reporting a substantial violation of law.' That is the protective clause. And Section 5(j)(iv) requires MITRE to make every subcontractor and consultant sign a non-disclosure agreement containing the Section 9(g) terms 'with the exception of Section 9(g)(2).' The people at the outer edge of the work - the ones brought in for specialised expertise MITRE does not hold in-house - are contractually bound by the secrecy terms without the clause that preserves their right to tell Congress.

This is the structural argument, and on 22 May 2026 a member of Congress made it out loud. Rep. Eric Burlison, of the House Oversight Committee's Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, sent a ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests to MITRE's president Mark Peters and its general counsel Christopher Land. The relevant time period is 'January 1, 1930, to the present.' The definitions section reaches every MITRE-operated FFRDC, every subcontractor, and any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, or equivalent terms.'

The interrogatories are targeted at exactly the mechanism described above. Section III demands identification of every Special Access Program, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword and DOE SIGMA category MITRE participated in or supported in connection with UAP records, and asks whether each 'was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks MITRE to identify any classification guide, NDA, access roster or sponsor communication that instructed personnel to avoid using the terms UAP, UFO, crash retrieval or reverse engineering in records. Section VIII asks for every NDA or indoctrination instrument 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations that restricted MITRE personnel from reporting UAP-related matters to Congress.' Section IX asks MITRE to identify any UAP-related work involving Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems or Bigelow Aerospace. Section X asks whether responsive funding was routed through a cover programme 'whose public description differed materially from the responsive work performed.' The letter warns that concealment or destruction may implicate 18 U.S.C. sections 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519 and 2071.

MITRE's reply, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was a single sentence from a spokesperson: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That answer is not evasive so much as accurate. It restates the architecture the letter was written to expose. An FFRDC's disclosure obligation runs to its sponsor. Congress asks MITRE; MITRE asks the sponsor; the sponsor is the same authority that classified the work. What the record does not contain, as of this writing, is the certification of search methodology, the records-location index, the preservation hold, or any production - all of which the letter demanded on 30- and 45-day clocks.
openQuestions: Did MITRE issue the preservation hold demanded within ten business days, and if so, which systems, archives and air-gapped environments does it cover?

Whether the subcontractor/consultant NDA construction found in the DHS HS SEDI sponsoring agreement - Section 9(g) secrecy terms without the Section 9(g)(2) congressional-disclosure carve-back - also appears in the sponsoring agreements for MITRE's DoD, FAA, Treasury, HHS and NIST FFRDCs, which are not public in comparable form.
Which federal sponsor would have to authorise release of any responsive MITRE record, and whether any sponsor has been asked.

Whether MITRE's National Security Engineering Center or its work for the FAA ever handled UAP sensor, radar or anomaly-detection data, which Section V of the interrogatories asks about directly and which has not been answered publicly.
MITRE's role in administering JASON, and whether JASON was ever tasked on UAP or anomalous materials questions, is not addressed anywhere in the public record reviewed here.
dossier.whatItIs: The MITRE Corporation is a private not-for-profit spun out of MIT Lincoln Laboratory in 1958 that operates exclusively as a manager of federally funded research and development centers. It runs six FFRDCs on behalf of the Department of Defense, the Federal Aviation Administration, Treasury and the IRS, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Health and Human Services, and NIST. It is headquartered in McLean, Virginia, and also provides the administrative home for JASON, the government's standing outside scientific advisory panel.
dossier.whyImplicated: MITRE is on this map because of the legal mechanism it embodies, not because a witness has named it as a custodian of material. An FFRDC is granted, by regulation, access to government and contractor data 'beyond that which is common to the normal contractual relationship' - including sensitive and proprietary data, installations, equipment and real property - and its sponsoring agreement gives the sponsor's Executive Agent approval authority over the classification, publication and distribution of its output. That combination produces a private organisation holding federal program records under a disclosure obligation that runs to a sponsoring agency rather than to Congress or to the public, and whose corporate files are not agency records for FOIA purposes. The DHS sponsoring agreement goes further: MITRE's own staff sign non-disclosure agreements that expressly preserve the right to report substantial violations of law to Congress, but subcontractors and consultants are required to sign the same NDA with that whistleblower carve-back removed. On 22 May 2026 Rep. Eric Burlison put this exact structure in writing, telling MITRE that FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records' and demanding a search back to 1 January 1930.

entityInfo.desc: FY2024 FFRDC funding places MITRE's National Security Engineering Center at approximately $1,431.7 million, ahead of the Aerospace FFRDC ($1,309.8 million) and MIT Lincoln Laboratory ($1,360.6 million), and behind only the DOE weapons and multiprogram laboratories - Sandia ($4,584.0 million), Los Alamos ($3,918.3 million), JPL ($2,647.8 million), Livermore ($2,188.8 million), Oak Ridge ($2,091.2 million), Idaho ($1,594.1 million) and Pacific Northwest ($1,585.7 million). MITRE's total corporate revenue passed $2.37 billion in 2023. Contract vehicles documented on USAspending: NSEC through Army Contracting Command IDIQ W56KGU18D0004 with annual task orders W56KGU20F0009 ($583m), W56KGU21F0008 ($618m), W56KGU22F0017 ($687m), W56KGU23F0006 ($731m) and W56KGU24F0010 ($752m); CAASD through FAA contracts DTFAWA10C00080 ($1.70bn) and 693KA822C00001 ($761m). Governance since 2015: Rodney E. Slater, former Secretary of Transportation, as board chair; Donald Kerr, former Los Alamos director, NRO director and Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, elected chairman in November 2018 with former House Intelligence Committee chairman Mike Rogers as vice chairman; Sue Gordon, former Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence, joining in 2021 and elected vice chair on 31 October 2023; Paul Kaminski, former Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Technology, retiring from the board in 2025; Samantha Ravich, former vice chair of the President's Intelligence Advisory Board, elected 19 May 2026. Executive leadership: Mark Peters (President and CEO, from Battelle), Dana Keoki Jackson (SVP and GM, MITRE National Security, from Lockheed Martin's CTO office), Charles Clancy (CTO), Greg Crawford (Deputy GM, National Security), Austin Wang (VP, Intelligence Center), Yosry Barsoum (VP, Center for Securing the Homeland), Christopher Land (General Counsel and Secretary to the Board). That last title matters procedurally: the officer who determines MITRE's legal response to a congressional production request is the same officer who serves as secretary to the board chaired and vice-chaired by former senior intelligence officials.
